name: RE# (Resharp)
workload: BurntSushi/rebar benchmark suite: finding all matches for baseline categories (literal, words, bounded-repeat, ReDoS, quadratic, date/dictionary) plus extended categories (monster regexes, character sets, Unicode, lookarounds), comparing against Rust regex, RE2, PCRE2, and Hyperscan
claimed_speedup: Paper (POPL 2025 / arXiv 2407.20479) states RE# is 'over 71% faster than the next fastest engine Rust' on rebar baseline benchmarks (~2.54 vs 1.48, derived from page data), and 'outperforms all other engines and often by several orders of magnitude' on extended benchmarks. Repo README separately shows RE# 37x-34,833x faster than .NET's own Compiled/SourceGenerated regex engines on curated rebar patterns.
tradeoffs: .NET/F# only (companion from-scratch Rust reimplementation exists at github.com/ieviev/resharp but author says it is currently slower than the F# version); extends regex syntax with intersection (&), complement (~(...)), and universal wildcard (_) beyond standard .NET regex; uses leftmost-longest match semantics, not PCRE-style leftmost-first
caveats: The 71%-faster-than-Rust figure comes from the peer-reviewed paper's rebar-based evaluation table, which we could not fully re-open (PDF/HTML extraction was partial); exact CPU model and compiler/runtime versions for that specific Rust-regex comparison were not confirmed. The README's own benchmark table (AMD Ryzen 7 5800X, .NET 10.0) only compares RE# against .NET's built-in engines, not against Rust regex/RE2/PCRE2.
found_via: arXiv: 'regular expression matching faster than RE2 PCRE2 SIMD automata paper' -> RE#: High Performance Derivative-Based Regex Matching with Intersection, Complement, and Restricted Lookarounds (arXiv 2407.20479, POPL 2025 / ACM DOI 10.1145/3704837)

name: coregex
workload: Cross-language benchmark (kolkov/regex-bench) on a 6.0 MB generated text file across 16 real-world patterns (inner literal, IP address, email, URI, multiline PHP path, version string, suffix, literal alternation, HTTP methods, multi-literal, char class, word-repeat, anchored), using FindAll for a fair cross-engine comparison
claimed_speedup: Up to 52x faster than Rust regex on inner-literal patterns (0.26ms vs 13.55ms); 17.6x faster on IP-address matching; 7.7x faster on suffix patterns; 2.0x faster on multiline patterns; but 1.8x-7.4x SLOWER than Rust regex on 7 of the 16 tested patterns (email, uri, literal_alt, http_methods, multi_literal, alpha_digit, word_digit, word_repeat)
tradeoffs: Requires Go 1.25+; AVX2/SSSE3 SIMD paths are AMD64-only with a pure-Go fallback elsewhere; results are pattern-dependent, winning on literal-prefilterable patterns and losing on alternation-heavy or bounded-repeat patterns compared to Rust's mature Teddy/DFA implementation
caveats: Benchmark repo (kolkov/regex-bench) shares the same author/ecosystem as coregex, so this is effectively a first-party benchmark despite being a separate repo; Rust regex crate version and build flags (release mode, opt-level) are not stated; README explicitly notes results vary +/-30% due to CI VM load, and the widely-quoted '3-3000x' headline figure is against Go's stdlib regexp, not against Rust regex.
found_via: WebSearch: 'regex engine benchmark faster than std::regex Rust regex 2025 2026' -> dev.to 'From 100x Slower Than Rust to Beating It: The coregex Journey' -> github.com/coregx/coregex

name: BLARE (Blazingly Fast Regular Expression)
workload: Regex matching over 2 Microsoft-internal production workloads and 1 public workload (US-Accidents Kaggle dataset), decomposing each regex into components evaluated via a multi-armed-bandit-selected, non-left-to-right execution plan, implemented on top of RE2, PCRE2, Boost Regex, and ICU Regex
claimed_speedup: 1.6x-3.7x faster than RE2; 3.4x-7.9x faster than Boost Regex; 3.1x to over 100x faster than PCRE2 (as reported in the paper abstract)
compiler_and_flags: g++ >= 8.4.0, cmake >= 3.14 (build requirements per repo; exact flags used to produce the paper's reported numbers not confirmed)
tradeoffs: Research prototype built as a layer on top of RE2/PCRE2/Boost/ICU rather than a standalone engine; requires linking Abseil, Boost, ICU, and PCRE2; the repo's own README warns the current main-branch code 'may not produce results identical to that in the BLARE paper' and points to a separate original_codebase/BLARE_CODE folder to reproduce the exact published numbers
caveats: No LICENSE file exists in the repository (GitHub reports license: none), so the code is all-rights-reserved by default despite being public; the full ACM PDF returned HTTP 403 so we could not confirm the exact CPU model/compiler flags behind the headline numbers; only 9 GitHub stars and no commits in ~2.8 years.
found_via: WebSearch: 'regular expression matching faster than RE2 PCRE2 SIMD automata paper' -> BLARE (Blazingly Fast Regular Expression), ACM PACMMOD, DOI 10.1145/3589297

name: rejit
workload: DNA-matching benchmark from the Computer Language Benchmarks Game (regex-dna) at input sizes from 500KB to 500MB, multi-threaded Rejit vs RE2; also a recursive `grep -R` over the Linux 3.10.6 kernel source tree vs GNU grep 2.14
claimed_speedup: ~1.4x-1.8x faster than RE2 across all tested DNA-matching input sizes (e.g. 50MB: RE2 1.629s vs Rejit 0.971s = 1.68x faster, derived from page data; 500MB: RE2 20.693s vs Rejit 11.594s = 1.78x faster, derived from page data); also 1.68x faster than GNU grep 2.14 on the kernel-source grep task
hardware: Intel Core i5-2400 @ 3.10GHz (quad-core), 4GiB RAM, Fedora 17 (kernel 3.8.13-100.fc17.x86_64), SSE4.2
tradeoffs: x86_64-only, requires SSE4.2; unmaintained prototype/proof-of-concept, not production-hardened; benchmark hardware (2011-era CPU) and RE2 build (~2013 commit) are over a decade old so results may not reflect current RE2 performance
caveats: GitHub's automatic license detector reports 'NOASSERTION' for this repo even though the README explicitly states the project is GPLv3-licensed; treat the license as needing manual confirmation. No commits since 2015; benchmark numbers are ~13 years old and RE2 has been heavily optimized since.
found_via: WebSearch: 'SIMD regex engine paper faster than RE2 throughput' -> GitHub - coreperf/rejit: fast SIMD-able JIT regular expression compiler
